title: From Pixels to Policy: An Earth Observation Hackathon
text:
Welcome
This website hosts the materials for From Pixels to Policy: An Earth Observation Hackathon, a one-day, hands-on event where you’ll brainstorm and code your way through some of the most pressing heat and greenspace challenges facing a UK city region.
The hackathon is organised by Imago: Data Service for Imagery in collaboration with the Earth Observation Data Hub (EODH) and the North East Data Network (DataNEt) at Insights North East (INE). It brings together local authority professionals, policy experts and data/technical practitioners to explore how satellite imagery and Earth observation (EO) data can inform local responses to urban heat, greenspace and unequal exposure in Newcastle and the wider North East.

title: From Pixels to Policy: An Earth Observation Hackathon
text:
Who is this for?
Policy & public sector participants. Local authority officers, policy makers and public health practitioners interested in new data sources, or in fresh ways of working with environmental and spatial data. You don’t need to code — your knowledge of how decisions actually get made is what turns a map into a policy.
Technical participants. Data scientists, programmers and GIS/geographic data specialists who want to collaborate on practical, hands-on data challenges using Earth observation products from Imago and the EODH.
Teams are deliberately mixed so that every group combines policy and operational knowledge with analytical capability.

title: Overview
text:
Themes
Cities in the UK are being asked to plan for hotter summers. Local authorities need to know which neighbourhoods overheat, who lives there, and where new trees or parks would do the most good — but the evidence to answer these questions is often patchy, out of date, too coarse to show differences between neighbourhoods, or locked in specialist formats.
Earth observation (EO) data offers a different way in. Satellites measure land surface temperature, vegetation and land cover repeatedly and consistently, across every neighbourhood at once. Turned into the right indicators and joined to the geographies councils already use, these “pixels” can inform everyday policy decisions.
From Pixels to Policy is a one-day hackathon that tests this idea on real challenges in Newcastle and the wider North East Mayoral Strategic Authority. Mixed teams of policy and technical participants will work with data from Imago and the Earth Observation Data Hub (EODH) to produce outputs that a local authority could actually use.
Each theme has a problem statement; teams choose one and confirm it at the team meeting on 30 November.

title: Overview
text:
Theme
Example questions

What sets the hottest neighbourhoods apart from the coolest?


Greenspace and cooling

Unequal exposure

title: Overview
text:
Partners
Imago: Data Service for Imagery (imago.ac.uk) is a Smart Data Research UK (SDR UK) data service, funded by UKRI, that turns satellite imagery into ready-to-use data products for social science and policy research. Imago brings together research teams at the Universities of Liverpool and Newcastle and at Harvard.
The Earth Observation Data Hub (EODH) (eodatahub.org.uk) is a single point of access to UK Earth observation data and processing infrastructure. It is led by the National Centre for Earth Observation (NCEO) and funded by NERC with the UK Space Agency. Participants will use EODH workspaces to find, access and analyse data on the day.
Insights North East (INE) (insightsnortheast.co.uk) is a collaborative hub for place-based policy insights, based at Newcastle University. Its North East Data Network (DataNEt), co-created with the North East Mayoral Strategic Authority, connects data experts with policymakers and decision-makers across the region.

title: The Hackathon Day
text:
Session details

10:00–10:30 — Welcome and framing
Why Earth observation for local policy, what Imago and the EODH provide, and how the day connects to the North East’s priorities on heat and greenspace.



10:30–12:30 — Sprint 1
Teams agree a focused question within their problem statement, explore the data in their EODH workspace and start building. Mentors from Imago and the EODH circulate to help with data access and methods; policy participants help keep the work anchored to a real decision.


13:15–13:30 — Mid-point stand-up
Each team gives a two-minute update: what question you’re answering, what’s working and what’s blocking you.


13:30–15:00 — Sprint 2
Finish the analysis, make the output readable for a non-technical audience and prepare a short presentation.


15:00–16:00 — Presentations and close
Each team presents for 5 minutes with 2 minutes of questions. Policy partners reflect on which outputs feel most useful and how they might be taken forward.

Mentors and judges
Mentors. Each team is supported through the day by mentors from Imago and the EODH, who help with data access, methods and code, and by policy mentors who help keep the work anchored to a real decision. Mentors also join the team meeting on 30 November and the EODH session on 2 December.
Judges. A small panel of policy and technical partners will watch the presentations and give feedback. They will look for:

Relevance: does the output answer a question a council or public health team actually needs answered?
Use of the data: is the data used sensibly, at a scale that suits the question?
Honesty: are the limits of the data and method clear?
Clarity: could a non-technical decision-maker understand and act on it?

title: Hackathon Challenges
text:
Participation
Over one day, your team will tackle a real local question about urban heat and greenspace using Earth observation data. Each team chooses one of the three problem statements below and confirms its choice at the team meeting on Monday 30 November. The strongest outputs will answer a question someone in a council or public health team actually needs answered, and be honest about what the data can and can’t show.
All teams work in their EODH workspace with the datasets listed on the Data page. Every dataset is available to every team: each problem statement suggests a core set and other options, but you are free to mix them.
Teams are pre-assigned and deliberately mixed. Each team includes at least one policy or public sector participant and two or three technical participants, supported by mentors from Imago and the EODH (see Mentors and judges). Policy participants frame the question and judge usefulness; technical participants make the data work. Both are essential.

title: Hackathon Challenges
text:
Study area
Start with Newcastle upon Tyne. Teams who want a wider view can scale up to the North East Mayoral Strategic Authority area: Newcastle, Gateshead, North Tyneside, South Tyneside, Sunderland, County Durham and Northumberland. That lets you compare dense urban cores with suburbs, towns and rural areas. All datasets cover the full area.

See the Case Study for counts by local authority.






Important



Choosing your scale

Few areas at MSOA level in Newcastle. With only 34 MSOAs, a correlation or model at MSOA level rests on 34 points, and splitting them into groups leaves very few in each. If you stay in Newcastle and want to estimate a relationship (challenges 2 and 3), work at LSOA level (180 areas), or scale up to the North East (253 MSOAs, 1,257 LSOAs).
Comparisons work well in Newcastle. Picking out the hottest and coolest few MSOAs from 34 (challenge 1) is manageable. Scaling up adds town and rural contrasts rather than statistical power.
Keep pixels local. The NCEO 100 m data are daily files across five summers. At North East scale that is a lot of data to process in a day without parallel computing. Use the Imago MSOA and LSOA products for the North East, and the pixels for Newcastle or a smaller pilot area.

title: Hackathon Challenges
text:
1. What makes a hotspot?

Theme: Urban heat
Question: What sets the hottest neighbourhoods apart from the coolest in surface cover and built-up density? Start in Newcastle, then test whether the same features mark hotspots across the North East.
Core data

Imago Sentinel-3 heat indicators (MSOA), summer daytime, to pick out the hottest and coolest MSOAs.
Sentinel-2 summer composite (10 m), to describe them: vegetation (NDVI), built-up surfaces (NDBI) and water (NDWI).

Other options

Imago greenspace (LSOA) for share green.
HadUK-Grid air temperature (MSOA), to test whether hot surfaces also mean hot air.
Night-time Sentinel-3 indicators, to check whether daytime hotspots stay hot at night.
Population and deprivation table, to see who lives in the hotspots.

Go further

Choose a pilot area containing both hot and cool MSOAs and find hotspots within it at 100 m, using the Imago 100 m LSOA product or the NCEO 100 m pixels, instead of treating whole MSOAs as hot or cool.
At North East scale, compare hotspot features in city centres, towns and rural areas.

By 16:00: The hottest and coolest areas, a side-by-side comparison of their surface cover and built-up density, and three or four examples illustrated with Sentinel-2 imagery.

title: Hackathon Challenges
text:
2. Does green cool?

Theme: Greenspace and cooling
Question: How strongly is vegetation linked to lower surface temperature, and where does that link break down? Does it hold beyond Newcastle, across the wider North East?
Core data

Imago Sentinel-3 heat indicators (MSOA), day and night.
NDVI from the Sentinel-2 summer composite, averaged for each area.
Imago greenspace (LSOA) as share green, rolled up to MSOA.

Other options

Imago Sentinel-3 heat indicators at LSOA.
HadUK-Grid air temperature (MSOA), to see whether greener areas also have cooler air.
Population and deprivation table, to describe the places where green doesn’t cool.

Go further

Estimate the LST–NDVI relationship at 100 m, using the NCEO 100 m pixels against NDVI resampled to 100 m, or the Imago 100 m LSOA product, and check whether it holds at both scales and both times of day.
At North East scale, test whether the relationship differs between urban and rural areas.

By 16:00: A plot of the LST–NDVI relationship for day and night, and a map of places that are hotter than their greenness predicts, with a short note on why for two or three of them.

title: Hackathon Challenges
text:
3. Who lives in the heat?

Theme: Unequal exposure
Question: Is exposure to daytime and night-time heat unequal across social groups, and how much of the gap is linked to differences in greenspace? Compare Newcastle with the North East as a whole.
Core data

Imago Sentinel-3 heat indicators (MSOA), day and night.
Imago greenspace (LSOA) and NDVI from Sentinel-2.
The population and deprivation table (LSOA), aggregated to MSOA and weighted by population.

Other options

HadUK-Grid air temperature (MSOA), including heat extremes, as a measure closer to what people feel. It also has cold extremes, so you can check whether the same groups are exposed to both heat and cold.
Imago Sentinel-3 heat indicators at LSOA.

Go further

Work at LSOA level with the Imago 100 m LSOA product, joined directly to greenspace and the LSOA table.
Use the NCEO 100 m pixels to look at day-to-day variation during hot spells in specific neighbourhoods.

By 16:00:

Heat exposure gaps for two or three groups (for example most vs least deprived areas, older residents, social renters).
A simple model showing how each gap changes once greenspace is accounted for.
A one-slide policy summary for Insights North East. It should note that these are area-level patterns, not measures of what individuals experience.









Note



Outputs and recognition
All participant contributions incorporated into future published work will be acknowledged. Selected outputs will be showcased as data stories in the Book of Imagery or on the Imago blog, and may be developed further with Imago and our partners after the event. See Outputs for what each team should produce.

title: Case Study: Newcastle and the North East
text:
Why Newcastle?
The hackathon starts from Newcastle upon Tyne. Working on one city lets teams go deep on local detail, use the geographies the council already works with, and produce outputs that local partners can recognise and test against what they know on the ground. Teams can scale up to the North East Mayoral Strategic Authority area to compare the city with its neighbours, towns and rural areas.
crumbs: Case Study: Newcastle and the North East

title: Case Study: Newcastle and the North East
text:
A mix of urban forms. Dense terraced and inner-city neighbourhoods, large post-war estates, suburbs, river corridor, and major green spaces such as the Town Moor and Jesmond Dene all sit within one local authority. That mix produces real variation in heat and greenspace.
Strong local partnerships. Insights North East and the North East Data Network connect researchers directly with local authority and public health teams, so problem statements come from real policy needs.
Heat in a cool region. The North East is among the cooler parts of England, which keeps cold exposure a live public health concern, yet hot spells still produce marked differences in heat between neighbourhoods, and a region less used to heat may be less prepared for it.
A regional comparison. The wider North East adds Gateshead, Sunderland, the Tyneside boroughs, County Durham and Northumberland, from dense urban cores to market towns and rural areas.

title: Data
text:
1. Data Access
This page lists the datasets for the hackathon and where to find documentation. The challenges describe what the data are for; read both before the team meeting on 30 November.
The data fall into three groups: Imago products already summarised to policy geographies, pixel-level Earth observation data for teams who want to build their own indicators, and supporting layers loaded for every team as context.
All hackathon data will be in your team’s EODH workspace, ready to open in a Python Jupyter notebook. Set up your account by following Getting Started with EODH before the 2 December session. The EODH platform does not display uploaded datasets as maps, so plan to view them in a notebook.
Imago’s UK-wide products can also be browsed in the Imago Data Catalogue, currently a preview release.

title: Data
text:
Tip



Starter notebooks
Example Python notebooks for loading and exploring these datasets are in the tutorial/ folder of the GitHub repository. See Hackathon notebooks and data for the full list.

title: Data
text:
2. Datasets

2.1 Imago products
Imago produces satellite-derived data products for social science and policy research, summarised to small areas so they can be joined directly to population and deprivation data.

Land surface temperature heat indicators, Sentinel-3 (MSOA). Summer heat indicators for every MSOA in the UK, built from Sentinel-3 land surface temperature (~1 km pixels), 2019–2024. Summer night-time mean and median are being finalised, and daytime mean and median will be added. The underlying Sentinel-3 product is in the Imago Data Catalogue.
Land surface temperature heat indicators, Sentinel-3 (LSOA). The same indicators at LSOA level, prepared for the hackathon. In dense urban areas many LSOAs are smaller than a single 1 km pixel, so neighbouring LSOAs can share the same value. Comparing this with the 100 m product below is a useful exercise in its own right.
Land surface temperature heat indicators, 100 m (LSOA). An educational product built by Imago for the hackathon from the NCEO 100 m land surface temperature data (section 2.2), 2020–2024. Summer night-time mean and median, with daytime mean and median to follow. The finer source resolution captures street- and neighbourhood-level differences that the 1 km product misses.
Air temperature indicators, HadUK-Grid (MSOA). Met Office 1 km gridded air temperature, 2015–2024, summarised into annual and seasonal indicators and heat and cold extremes. Use these to compare surface with air temperature, or to bring in cold extremes alongside heat.
Greenspace (LSOA). A UK-wide greenspace product based on a binary green / non-green classification of satellite imagery, summarised to LSOA.







Tip



Land surface temperature is not air temperature. Land surface temperature measures how hot the ground and roofs are; air temperature is closer to what people feel. The two are related but can differ a lot, especially by day. The hackathon gives you both.




2.2 Pixel-level Earth observation data
For teams who want to build their own indicators or go below LSOA level.

Land surface temperature, 100 m (NCEO). Gridded land surface temperature at 100 m from the National Centre for Earth Observation’s Surface Temperature Group at the University of Leicester. Daily day and night files (NetCDF), 2020–2024, on a latitude/longitude grid (EPSG:4326), covering the North East (bounding box −2.69, 54.45 to −1.24, 55.81). Values are in Kelvin: subtract 273.15 for °C. Reproject to British National Grid (EPSG:27700) before measuring distances or areas.
Sentinel-2 (EODH). Open 10 m multispectral imagery from the EODH catalogue, provided as a single cloud-free summer composite matched to the land surface temperature period. Use the red and near-infrared bands to compute vegetation indices such as NDVI. Newcastle imagery for summers 2019–2026 is also discoverable in the EODH catalogue if you want to go further.







Important



Credit and use. Any output using the 100 m land surface temperature data, or the Imago 100 m LSOA product derived from it, must credit the NCEO Leicester Surface Temperature Group. These data are provided for use in the hackathon workspaces only and must not be shared outside the event.


Documentation: EODH documentation · Getting Started with EODH · EODH FAQs


2.3 Supporting layers
Loaded for every team as context:

LSOA and MSOA boundaries (2021), from the Imago Data Catalogue: LSOA boundaries for the United Kingdom (2021). A North East-only copy, ne_lsoa_2021_boundaries.gpkg, is in the repository’s data/ folder.
Population and deprivation tables for the North East, to show who lives in the hottest, coldest and least green places:

ne_lsoa_population_imd.csv (1,257 LSOAs): Census 2021 population, residents aged 0–4, 65+ and 75+, household tenure (owned, social rented, private rented), and the Index of Multiple Deprivation 2025 score, rank and decile, with the Income, Health, Living Environment and older-people income deprivation domains.
ne_msoa_population_imd.csv (253 MSOAs): the same aggregated to MSOA, with population-weighted deprivation scores and the share of residents in England’s most deprived 20% of LSOAs.
ne_population_imd_variables.csv: a description of every column. Full definitions are in data/VARIABLES.md.


These tables are in the data/ folder of the repository and will be in your workspace. The Python notebook that builds them, with step-by-step notes, is in scripts/ if you want to see how they were made. Its last two sections have starter plots and worked examples of merging these tables with the Imago products.

title: Outputs
text:
Expected Outputs
With only one day, aim for one clear answer to one well-framed question rather than a complete analysis. Each team produces one of the following, depending on its challenge:
1. A hotspot comparison (What makes a hotspot?)
The hottest and coolest areas, a side-by-side comparison of their surface cover and built-up density, and three or four examples illustrated with Sentinel-2 imagery.
2. A greenness–temperature analysis (Does green cool?)
A plot of the land surface temperature–NDVI relationship for day and night, and a map of places that are hotter than their greenness predicts, with a short note on why for two or three of them.
3. A heat inequality brief (Who lives in the heat?)
Heat exposure gaps for two or three social groups, a simple model showing how each gap changes once greenspace is accounted for, and a one-slide policy summary for Insights North East.
Outputs can take whatever form best communicates the findings: a static map with a short brief, a notebook, a simple dashboard or an interactive map.

title: Outputs
text:
Presentation
Each team gives a 5-minute presentation (maximum 5 slides) at the end of the day, followed by 2 minutes of questions. The judges will give feedback on relevance, use of the data, honesty about limits and clarity. A good presentation covers:

The question — what decision does this support, and for whom?
The data — what you used and why
The finding — the one thing a decision-maker should take away
The caveats — what the data can’t tell you
Next steps — what would make this usable in practice

Teams are encouraged to share their code and outputs in a GitHub repository.

title: Outputs
text:
After the hackathon
Imago will showcase outputs from the day as data stories in the Book of Imagery or on the Imago blog. Teams whose work is featured will be credited and invited to help shape the story. To make this easy:

keep your notebook tidy and runnable from top to bottom;
save your key map or figure as an image;
write two or three sentences on the finding and what it means for policy.







Note



Recognition
All team contributions incorporated into future published work will be acknowledged. Promising outputs may be developed further with Imago, the EODH and Insights North East after the event.

title: Resources
text:
Hackathon notebooks and data
A curated list of tutorials, courses and software for working with Earth observation and geographic data in Python. The hackathon supports Python only: the EODH workspaces run Python notebooks, and the mentors will support Python code on the day.
Starter notebooks and ready-to-use data for the hackathon are in the GitHub repository. The same materials will be preloaded in your team’s EODH workspace, and we’ll walk through them at the 2 December session.
You don’t need a GitHub account to view or download them: open a notebook on GitHub to read it, or use Code → Download ZIP on the repository page to get everything.

title: Resources
text:
tutorial/: example Python notebooks, each following the same steps (load, explore, analyse, visualise):

01_air_temperature.ipynb: Imago air temperature (MSOA)
02_rgb_greens.ipynb: RGB greenspace (LSOA)
05_eodh_data_access.ipynb: accessing Sentinel-2 ARD and Landsat LST through EODH
Notebooks for Sentinel-3 LST (~1 km) and NCEO LST (~100 m) will be added once those datasets are ready.

data/: North East boundaries and population/deprivation tables, with column definitions in VARIABLES.md. See the Data page for the full list.
scripts/: the annotated notebooks used to prepare the data, if you want to see how it was made.

title: Resources
text:
Geographic Data Science

A course in Geographic Data Science — the ENVS363/563 module from the Geographic Data Science Lab, University of Liverpool, with Python labs covering spatial data, mapping vector and raster data, spatial weights, ESDA and clustering.
Advanced Geovisualisation — Python-based geovisualisation; useful for teams building interactive maps.

title: Resources
text:
Python

Mapping and Data Visualization with Python — Spatial Thoughts course covering GeoPandas, XArray, interactive maps with Folium and Leafmap, and dashboards with Streamlit. Notebooks run in Google Colab.
rioxarray and rasterstats — reading rasters and computing zonal statistics (e.g. mean temperature per LSOA).
pystac-client — searching STAC catalogues for satellite scenes.


Hackathon Python environment
The workspaces will include the core packages below. Getting comfortable with a few of them before the day will help.

Data processing: numpy, pandas, xarray, scipy
Geospatial analysis: rasterio, rioxarray, geopandas, shapely, pyproj, rasterstats
Earth observation and data access: pystac-client, pyeodh, odc-stac, requests, fsspec, s3fs
Visualisation and machine learning: matplotlib, scikit-learn, folium
Scientific data formats: netCDF4, h5netcdf
